title: Stroke (Cerebrovascular Accident)
lead: Rebuilding movement after brain injury: assessment, recovery and task-specific training.
case: A 64-year-old man is 10 days after a left middle cerebral artery ischaemic stroke. He has right arm weakness (some wrist extension), right leg weakness, expressive aphasia, and can sit unsupported but needs help of one to stand. BP stable within targets. Goal: walk to the bathroom.

> Plan: repeated sit-to-stand, standing balance tasks, assisted walking practice with a frame or therapist, right arm task practice (reaching, grasping cups), simple gestures and demonstrations to overcome aphasia.
plan: repeated sit-to-stand, standing balance tasks, assisted walking practice with a frame or therapist, right arm task practice (reaching, grasping cups), simple gestures and demonstrations to overcome aphasia.
qa: Why use demonstrations with this patient? Expressive aphasia mainly affects speaking; comprehension may be better, but short instructions with demonstration are clearer.
Which arm intervention could be considered later? Constraint-induced movement therapy, because he has some active wrist extension.
How do you protect his shoulder? Support the arm, avoid pulling, position carefully, educate carers.
Which measure do you take weekly for walking? Gait speed (10-metre walk test).
He suddenly develops slurred speech and facial droop in therapy. Action? Emergency: possible new stroke; call the medical team and record the time.

redFlags.Finding: New face, arm or speech change, sudden vision loss or imbalance
redFlags.Immediate action: Call emergency team; note time of onset

redFlags.Finding: BP above the medically agreed limit, severe headache
Coughing or wet voice during eating or drinking, fever
Hot, swollen painful hand and wrist

manual.name: Facilitated movement (guiding the patient through a task)
manual.why: Help the patient feel a correct movement
manual.finding: Early, when the patient cannot move alone
manual.application: Reduce help as soon as possible; active practice is the aim

manual.name: Weight-bearing through the weak arm in sitting
manual.why: Sensory input, trunk and arm support

manual.name: Shoulder handling
manual.application: Never pull on the weak arm; support the arm at all times

exercise.Intervention: Reaching tasks in sitting outside the base of support
exercise.Example starting dose: 3 sets of 10 reaches in different directions

exercise.Intervention: Repeated sit-to-stand from a raised seat, lowering seat height as able
Progressive resistance training (step-ups, leg press, bridging)
exercise.Example starting dose: 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12, 2 to 3 times a week

exercise.Intervention: Overground walking practice, treadmill with or without body-weight support, circuit class training

exercise.Problem: Arm with some wrist and finger movement
exercise.Intervention: Constraint-induced movement therapy (restrain the strong arm, intensive use of the weak arm)
exercise.Example starting dose: Hours of practice per day in structured programs

exercise.Intervention: Mirror therapy, electrical stimulation, mental practice, bilateral tasks

exerciseNotes: Core principles: task-specific, repetitive, progressively challenging, meaningful to the patient, and in high dose.
Waiting for "normal" movement before allowing functional practice slows recovery. Allow the patient to practise real tasks, giving feedback on safety and quality.

modalities.name: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) for foot drop or shoulder
modalities.comment: Improves walking or reduces subluxation in some patients

modalities.name: Ankle-foot orthosis
modalities.indicated: For foot drop and knee control

modalities.name: Shoulder supports
modalities.comment: Avoid long-term slings that encourage stiffness

modalities.name: Botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
modalities.comment: Combine with stretching and task practice

pathway: Acute (days): stability, positioning, swallowing awareness, early graded mobilisation, chest care, prevention of complications.
Subacute (weeks to months): intensive task-specific practice; most rapid recovery occurs in the first months.
Chronic (after about 6 months): continued gains possible with practice; fitness, community walking, secondary prevention (exercise, BP control).
